newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan aims to avert tragedy in Peru hostage crisis.
newsitem.headline: Japan aims to avert tragedy in Peru hostage crisis.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said on Thursday his weekend summit with Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori would confirm there would be no "caving in to terrorism" in solving the Peru hostage crisis.

The Japanese leader, however, is likely to temper that tough talk with a plea that Lima avoid steps that could prompt Marxist rebels to harm the 72 hostages they hold at the Japanese ambassador's residence, officials said.

Hashimoto, who several times this week voiced concern that Peruvian police security measures were provoking the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement guerrillas, will hold talks with Fujimori in Toronto on Saturday in a bid to coordinate views on the six-week-old standoff.

"With efforts to find a peaceful end to the hostage situation reaching a critical stage more than a month after it began, it is extremely important that the two leaders exchange views in direct talks," government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama told a morning news conference.

Kajiyama, asked in an an afternoon news conference if Hashimoto would pressure the Peruvian government not to use force, Kajiyama said: "The meeting is not meddling with the Peruvian government, but is a discussion."

Hashimoto must balance his desire to end the crisis soon against fears for the safety of the hostages, which include about two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats, including Ambassador Morihisa Aoki, analysts said.

Hashimoto said he was making the trip at Fujimori's request and that the two leaders will reconfirm the tough stance Tokyo and Lima have taken against the hostage-takers and seek the release of the hostages.

"I can't go into details at this delicate stage but what we must confirm is that we must not cave in to terrorism and at the same time seek the release of all captives unharmed and as soon as possible," Hashimoto told a parliamentary committee.
Kajiyama later said Hashimoto's remark on terrorism "does not mean we will take any means including risking the lives of the hostages."
The meeting in Toronto comes amid growing concern in Lima and Tokyo that with negotiations stalled, the crisis shows no signs of ending.

"It's been a month since it appeared that negotiations between the Peru government and the guerrillas would begin, but we're still stuck outside the doorway," said a Foreign Ministry official in Tokyo.
Efforts to start talks with the guerrillas have stalled over the main rebel demand of freedom for about 400 jailed comrades, which Fujimori has refused to discuss.
Hashimoto on Tuesday told Fujimori that Japan is worried that the hostages' lives could be endangered if pressure is stepped up on the roughly 15 armed members of MRTA.
In an apparent bid to weaken the rebels' resolve, police have blasted marching music at the residence in the early mornings and led processions of armoured vehicles around it.
The rebels, who have mined and booby-trapped the diplomatic residence, fired several bullets on Monday at police in a convoy of armoured cars, hitting one vehicle.
